title: Should USA Fans Feel Jilted Over Pochettino's Exit To Manchester United?
content:
Manchester United is one of the biggest clubs in the world. The pressure of being manager at Old Trafford is immense, but if you succeed, then you can become a legend. 

So why shouldn't Mauricio Pochettino, who led the U.S. men's national team at the 2026 World Cup, take on that challenge? And should USMNT fans feel some type of way for him bolting? 

"This is not surprising," Alexi Lalas said on his "State of the Union with Alexi Lalas" podcast. "Anybody that feels jilted, I think you're being naive." 

Pochettino is set to take over Man United, just months after signing a contract extension that meant to see him guide the USA through the 2030 World Cup. Instead, he'll head back to the Premier League and take on the task of guiding the historic but beleaguered club out of the relegation zone. 

It's hard for any manager not to want the job of guiding England's most successful club, but it is fair to question whether U.S. Soccer should have even given Pochettino a new deal. 

"It just feels a little disingenuous," said FOX Soccer analyst Stu Holden.

Man United executives, who fired Michael Carrick on Thursday, triggered the reported $10 million buyout clause in Pochettino's USMNT contract as well as an additional $2 million for the 54-year-old Argentine's coaching staff. 

Ever since Pochettino was hired by U.S. Soccer in October 2024, he has been linked to an eventual return to the European club circuit. He led Tottenham Hotspur to the 2019 Champions League final and later managed Chelsea for the 2023-24 season. He also won a Ligue 1 title with Paris Saint-Germain. 

Back in June before the World Cup, he was mentioned as a candidate for AC Milan – who decided to hire former United manager Ruben Amorim.

"He was very upfront and honest about this, so much so that there was even recognition in the contract on both sides. This is a creation of Mauricio Pochettino and the U.S. Soccer Federation," Lalas said. 

Holden had an interesting comparison about how this whole thing went down: "I feel like the side chick a little bit, in the way that we're just kind of hand in hand with Pochettino until the next big thing comes along." 

Of which Lalas responded: "With every side chick, everyone eventually takes them aside and asks, how did you not see this? How did you not see the signs?" 

Still, Holden added that he hopes it all works for Pochettino after guiding the USMNT to a round-of-16 appearance this summer at the World Cup. 

"Full disclosure, I really like Mauricio Pochettino, he's a good coach, he's got the vibes, he's got the aura. I hope he succeeds. But I feel like you always knew this would come soon, and it has come sooner than what you or everybody thought."

title: A Season-Saving Win: 3 Takeaways From Commanders Dramatic Victory Over Giants
content:
METLIFE STADIUM (East Rutherford, N.J.) — The New York Giants haven’t won the NFC East in 15 years, and they had a golden opportunity to take a big step towards ending that drought on Thursday night.

But then they blew it.

Despite leading the game with less than two minutes to go, they fell apart in crunch time as Jayden Daniels led the Washington Commanders on a late touchdown drive to pull out a dramatic 24-21 victory. They got the game-winning score on a laser pass through traffic from Daniels to Stefon Diggs that became a 32-yard touchdown with 57 seconds remaining.

The Giants had one last chance to pull it out, but J.J. McCarthy’s final pass on a solid night was intercepted.

And just like that, the NFC East looks like it might be a race again. The Giants fell to 5-3-1 on the season, closing the gap between them and the second-place Dallas Cowboys (4-5). And the Commanders, at 3-5-1, now hold the tie-breaker advantage over the Giants and are still in the thick of the race.

Here are my takeaways from the game that tightened this division up:
 

Over the last few weeks, Commanders QB Jayden Daniels has started to round into form, looking a little more like he did two years ago when he was a rookie sensation. That year, he carried a flawed team all the way to the NFC Championship Game.

This team, as hard as it is to believe, is even more flawed. But on Thursday night, he showed he’s capable of carrying them too.

Daniels was a one-man show at times against the Giants, completing 23 of 33 passes for 249 yards, with three touchdowns and two interceptions, and he ran 10 times for 28 yards, too. He kept the Giants’ punch-less defense on its heels with his ability to scramble. And when they left him unpressured in the pocket — all too often — he picked them apart with his arm.

Yeah, he threw two fourth-quarter interceptions, and that wasn’t good. It was also a product of the startling lack of weapons around him. Both passes were force-fed to TE Chig Okonkwo, who has been a disappointment for most of the season. To that point, it was a sign of how few players he had on the field around him who could make and break big plays.

But in the end, WR Stefon Diggs — the only receiver who can make big plays on the Commanders' active roster — came through. Diggs took a dart pass over the middle between a couple of Giants defenders, blasted free and ran in for the game-winning score. He finished with six catches for 83 yards.

Daniels has no other reliable weapons and no reliable running game and it just doesn’t matter. He’s a weapon all his own. He made it impossible for the Giants pass rush to catch him. He found receivers even when they weren’t open.

And just like he used to do so often as a rookie, Daniels reminded everyone he has the clutch gene and made the big play when it mattered most.

J.J. McCarthy has been mostly outstanding since the Giants acquired him from the Minnesota Vikings. He was terrific, for the most part, again on Thursday night.

But if he wants to make the Giants even think about choosing him over Jaxson Dart as their quarterback next season, he can’t afford to lose too many more games like this.

It wasn’t even about his game-ending interception. That was thrown out of desperation. It had more to do with the fact that even though he completed 22 of 36 passes for 294 yards and ran for 34 more yards, the offense shut down under his direction late in the fourth quarter when they could have put the game away. The Giants gave the Commanders life with two three-and-outs in the final 5.5 minutes.

That just won’t do.

The Giants are thrilled with McCarthy. They love his mobility. They're enthralled with his arm strength, as he showed in the fourth quarter with a bullet through double coverage to TE Isaiah Likely, which became a go-ahead, 66-yard touchdown pass. He’s doing most of everything they want. 

But he’s got a huge opportunity. The Giants have two 23-year-old potential franchise quarterbacks who will be under contract next season. They are committed to Dart, but they can just as easily change their commitment to McCarthy.

McCarthy will just have to do a lot more than he did on Thursday night to earn it.

The Giants’ top priority at the trade deadline was finding a defensive tackle who could not only help their leaky run defense, but also help them do the one thing they haven’t been able to do consistently since they lost edge rusher Brian Burns early in the season — pressure the quarterback.

Their inability to do that cost them dearly against Daniels on Thursday night, and it’s really going to hurt them as they play better teams and quarterbacks down the stretch and maybe into the postseason.

For most of the game, they couldn’t touch Daniels. Granted, he’s as elusive a quarterback as there is in the league, but the Giants made it easy on him. When he stayed in the pocket, he had plenty of time. When he escaped the pocket, it wasn’t because he was rushed, and there was nobody containing him on the outside.

As a result, he picked them apart with his arm, after picking them apart with his legs in a 27-27 tie last month.

The Giants rank near the bottom in the NFL with 17 sacks. They came into this game with a league-worst pressure rate of 18.9%. They’ve got Trevor Lawrence (Jacksonville), Brock Purdy (San Francisco), Jared Goff (Detroit) and Dak Prescott (Dallas) coming up over their next seven games.

It’s great that they’re opportunistic. They have a very strong secondary. And they had two more interceptions on Thursday night.

But the defense is really going to have to dial up the pressure against some of the NFL’s best quarterbacks to have a chance to survive.

It’s hard to overstate how much the Giants needed to pad their lead in the NFC East race on Thursday night, because this game marked the end point of the easy part of their schedule.

Up next for them is a minefield of the NFL’s elite, starting with the Jacksonville Jaguars in 10 days. And they’ll also face the San Francisco 49ers, the Seattle Seahawks, the Cleveland Browns and the Detroit Lions over the next seven weeks.

They are not quite in that class yet. And that could be a problem with the Cowboys now nipping at their heels.

As for the Commanders, they now have new life in the division race. They have a tough game against the Cincinnati Bengals when they return, but after that they have a very winnable two-game road trip to Arizona and Tennessee, where they’ll face two of the worst teams in the league.

That is a huge opportunity for them to make up some lost ground, and maybe really get into the thick of the race by the time they get to December.

title: Tom Brady Shares Ideal International Soccer Stadium To Host An NFL Game
content:
Tom Brady played in four international games over his decorated 23-year career. He played two in London before playing a game in Mexico City in 2017. He was also part of the NFL's first game in Germany, helping the Tampa Bay Buccaneers get a win in Munich in 2022.

But if Brady could have had authority over where to be sent for an international game, he would have selected a site that has yet to host an NFL game. 

"I would say San Siro in Italy, where AC Milan plays," Brady said when asked where he would most like to play an international game in the most recent edition of #AskTom. 

Brady attended San Siro to watch AC Milan play Como in February, and left with a lasting impression. 

"The way those Italian fans cheer all game long," he said. "I would have loved to play in front of them at least once in my career."

And Brady offered another Italian stadium that should host an NFL game. 

"Another bonus one: Lake Como," Brady said.

Lake Como, which is also known as Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia, is currently home to Como 1907, while the Italian men's national team occasionally plays matches there. The stadium is small, seating 13,600, but it's been called one of the most beautiful stadiums in the world for its lakeside view. 

As Brady seems to have a particular fondness for Italian stadiums, he couldn't help but envision what San Siro would be like if it hosted a game between heated divisional rivals, like the Cincinnati Bengals and Pittsburgh Steelers.

"That would be pretty frightening," Brady said. "It'd be like Mad Max escaped from LA. I'm not sure many of you guys would make it out of that stadium. It would be a complete zoo."

The NFL will head to Munich in Week 10 as Brady's former team, the New England Patriots, will face the Detroit Lions at Allianz Arena, home of FC Bayern Munich. It's the eighth international game of the 2026 season, and the only one in Germany. London has hosted three games. 

Melbourne, Rio de Janeiro, Paris and Madrid each hosted one earlier this year. Mexico City will host the ninth and final international game of the 2026 season in Week 11. 

The NFL has yet to travel to Italy for a game, but has expanded to add new cities each season. Milan could certainly be a site for the future. And while Brady wouldn't play in San Siro, he could certainly soak it in as a supporter of the sport. 

AC Milan currently sits fifth in the Italian Serie A table and has not won the league since 2021-22.

title: Italy Stuns France: 3 Takeaways From Thursday's Nations League Matches
content:
We had ourselves quite an evening of UEFA Nations League football. From euphoria at the San Siro and consistent Spanish omnipotence in Prague to the coronation of an English star at Wembley.

Here are my takeaways from Thursday’s action in the Nations League:

It was an incredibly important victory for Italy. Not perfect. Not beautiful. In fact, there were many mistakes, including another awful error from keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma and a missed penalty from one of the Esposito brothers in forward Sebastian. But none of that will matter because, in the end, under the skies of Milan and the iconic San Siro, Italy came out victorious thanks to a trait they know too well: passion and a will to get the job done.

There will of course be bigger evenings and nothing will heal the wounds of missing a third straight World Cup, but on a night where Roberto Mancini’s Azzurri wanted to make a statement against the mighty France, it ended with a smile on the faces of all Italians with a 3-1 victory thanks to grit and hunger.

It was a night of desire as opposed to substance as Italy relinquished possession but not control. Mancini’s decision to bring on Inter stalwart winger Federico Dimarco for Monza’s Nicolò Cambiaghi in the 62nd minute proved to be a masterstroke as it was his assist that provided the goal for midfielder Davide Frattesi. Another penalty was added and this time, striker Pio Esposito made it 3-1. 

Italy now sits atop of its group with a hope of getting something over Belgium in order to secure a place in the quarterfinals. France just needs a point, so despite the loss, manager Zinedine Zidane knows it sits in a good place as it gets ready for Türkiye. 

But tonight was about Italian poetry and, once again, Azurri rejoiced. It’s been a long time since we have seen that happen.

It wasn’t a 7-0 thrashing, but England came out with a 2-1 win over a valiant Croatia at Wembley, but the real story was an evening for superstar striker Harry Kane, who celebrated his record-breaking 126th appearance for the national team with a goal, scoring from the spot. 

Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers opened the scoring in the 24th-minute, but centerback Jarell Quansah allowed Croatia's Petar Sučić to equalize later in the second half.

But five minutes later, Kane, who paraded his Ballon d’Or in front of the Wembley crowd before the match, reclaimed the lead for the third-placed team at the World Cup.

This was also an evening of absences for England as Djed Spence, Ezri Konsa and Marc Guéhi all missed out, so defensively, Thomas Tuchel had to shuffle a few things. The German manager probably wanted a clean sheet, but when you have a rotated lineup of Lewis Hall, Dan Burn, the aforementioned Quansah and Trent Alexander-Arnold, I think he’ll be reasonably happy on defense. Hall, in particular, was very strong. 

But again, this was about Kane and an evening he will never forget. Next up? A mighty battle in Madrid against Spain.

The World Cup champions took care of business against Czechia thanks to a penalty from midfielder Alex Baena (one of my favorite players right now in Europe) and a stoppage-time second goal from Marc Pubill off the bench, both who play for Atlético de Madrid. That’s now 43 matches without a loss and 12 straight victories. A record so impressive, I am beginning to feel numb about Spanish results. I almost expect this side to win, no matter the outcome.

This wasn’t, however, a perfect painting from Luis de la Fuente’s side as a 1-0 lead stood throughout until the 96th minute. But then again, not all of them are going to be masterpieces and teams like Czechia will aim to make it sticky for a team who likes to play with the ball in an aesthetic rhythm. 

This was also a match without Lamine Yamal, Mikel Oyarzabal and the perennial leader, Rodri. Pedri, the team’s architect, didn’t even come on until the 76th minute. So we can see from tonight that it was a rotated side looking to keep the train moving against a weaker opponent.

And the table? Spain leads with a perfect 15 points from five matches, five wins, 13 goals scored and five conceded. What awaits now is a delicious battle at the Metropolitano as England visits the Spanish capital on Sunday. 

The host is the favorite, clearly, but I think if England is able to minimize its mistakes, it can maybe take something from the match. But asking an opponent to be perfect against Spain is the equivalent of swimming in an ocean during a storm. At some point, no matter how hard you fight, you will find yourself fighting against an overwhelming force that won’t let you breathe.

But if there’s a team that could maybe disrupt the artistry, as we saw in the last window, it’s England. It should be a fantastic match.

title: Robbie Avila Expected To Join TCU After Saint Louis Return Denied
content:
TCU is working to add center Robbie Avila to its roster after the former Saint Louis player was cleared to play by a judge but barred from returning to the Billikens due to roster restrictions.

Horned Frogs coach Jamie Dixon said Thursday he was contacted by Avila and his family after the fifth-year senior exhausted "all options to play at Saint Louis" and became aware of the injury situation at TCU. The Horned Frogs are without Texas Tech transfer Luke Bamgboye indefinitely.

Dixon said he had informed the team that the school was in the process of finalizing the eligibility of Avila, the reigning Atlantic 10 player of the year who became a sensation for his signature specs at Indiana State.

Avila was granted a fifth year under preliminary injunction, but the College Sports Commission ruled he couldn't play for Saint Louis due to the roster restrictions.

It was unlikely that Avila would be available for the Horned Frogs against Milwaukee on Friday night. Their next game is at home against Texas A&M on Nov. 19.

The Billikens won a school-record 29 games last season behind Avila, reaching the second round of the NCAA Tournament before losing to eventual national champion Michigan.

He averaged 12.8 points and 4.5 rebounds last season and has career averages of 14.5 points and 5.5 rebounds over four seasons — two each with Indiana State and Saint Louis.

The Horned Frogs are 3-0 but needed double overtime for a 100-92 victory over UL Monroe at home on Tuesday.

Reporting by the Associated Press.

title: Harry Kane An NFL Kicker? Patriots Star Drake Maye Supports It
content:
New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye fully endorses Harry Kane's dream of one day becoming an NFL kicker.

Maye spoke Thursday after practice at the campus of Bayern Munich — Kane's soccer team — ahead of Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions.

"It would be cool to see him try," Maye said. "He’s dealt with pressure, that's one of the biggest things about kicking in the National Football League is the pressure of it. He does that for a living. So, I don’t think he’d have any problem."

Kane, a longtime Patriots fan, recently became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or, soccer’s award for the best player in the world.

The 33-year-old England captain this month signed a contract extension to stay at Bayern until 2029, so it’s unclear when he’d be ready to give NFL kicking a shot.

Kane has mused over the years about trying it. He has even floated the idea of combining his NFL dream with joining a Major League Soccer team.

"I think I’ve seen him maybe kick a few, and he looked pretty good," Maye said. "No doubt, he does that for a living, so I’m sure he’d be just fine."

Jacksonville Jaguars kicker Cam Little weighed in on Kane a few days after booting a game-winning 57-yard field goal to beat the Philadelphia Eagles 19-17 in London a month ago. Little said Kane's biggest adjustment would be shifting from star striker to bit player. As a kicker, he said, "You’re out there just to back everyone up basically."

Bayern is still celebrating its first Ballon d’Or winner in 45 years. It’s also the first for any player at a German club since 1996.

Patriots tight end Hunter Henry said he doesn't know much about soccer but was well aware of the Bayern star: "He’s a dawg — lot of respect for Harry Kane."

Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: The Top-50 NFL Players In The First Half Of The 2026 Season, Ranked
content:
Who is the best player in the NFL? 

For the first handful of years of the 2020s, you could've easily answered that question by saying "Patrick Mahomes." But as the Kansas City Chiefs' star quarterback is in his first year back from an ACL tear, Mahomes isn't the shoo-in answer he once was to that question.

And there are plenty of quarterbacks who have staked their claim to be considered the best in the league so far in the 2026 season. And looking beyond the most important position in football, there are several other players who have dominated across the league over the first nine weeks of the year.

So, along with our eye in the sky Bucky Brooks, we ranked the top 50 players so far this season. We did use positional value to help shape the list, but quarterbacks don't entirely dominate our top 50. 

Steven Ruiz: Kyle Shanahan is trying his hardest to cut McCaffrey’s workload, but it’s difficult to resist the allure of giving him the football. When he’s out on the field, he’s been the focal point of the powerful 49ers offense. He’s still making defenders miss at a high rate, and he’s still getting open on every route he runs. Shanahan’s restraint over the first half should make McCaffrey even better over the second half of the season. 

Stat to know: McCaffrey has scored a touchdown in seven of his eight games this season (10 total touchdowns: nine rushing, one receiving). Following his 2,126-scrimmage-yard season in 2025, he has produced 27 total touchdowns in his last 25 regular-season games.

Henry McKenna: Carter just pops on film, with an explosiveness, disruptiveness and playmaking ability that the Giants must love. It has been fun to see Carter and Arvell Reese operate together as one of the most hard-to-handle young playmaking tandems in the NFL. New York has asked a lot of its defense in the early weeks of the season — what with the QB situation changing weekly. That has made Carter’s contributions all the most impressive.

Stat to know: Carter has generated 30 quarterback hits and six sacks in 25 games since entering the league with the Giants, recording at least one quarterback hurry or hit in 19 of those 25 appearances.

Ruiz: Williams can line up anywhere in Green Bay’s amorphous defense, and he seems to make plays wherever the Packers deploy him. He can be the last line of defense as a deep safety; drop into the box to defend the run; cover from the slot; or rush off the edge. He’s done it all at a high level in 2026. He’s made 48 tackles, intercepted three passes, defended seven more, and even generated 14 pressures as a pass rusher. 

Stat to know: Williams leads all Green Bay defensive backs with 71 total tackles and three interceptions through nine games, making him the only safety in the NFC this season with at least 70 tackles and 3+ interceptions.

McKenna: For all the splash plays that come from Jameson Williams and Gibbs, St. Brown is churning out catches and first downs when the team needs him most. It’s not always pretty. And it doesn’t always look impressive, given all the amazing stuff that the Lions do offensively. But St. Brown is one of the best and most reliable receivers in the NFL. Keep in mind: He had five touchdowns in the first three games. He hasn’t scored since. I think he’s overdue.

Stat to know: St. Brown has caught at least six passes in seven of Detroit's eight games this season. Coming off a 117-catch campaign in 2025, he has recorded five-plus receptions in 23 of his last 25 regular-season games.

Ruiz: The Bengals have spent the last few years trying to build a formidable pass protection for Joe Burrow, and Mims is the biggest hit yet. He’s looked impossible to beat in pass protection so far this season, allowing just five pressures across 319 pass snaps. Mims is a big, strong dude with quick feet, and his technique is always improving. His ability to hold up on an island is a big reason why Cincinnati can call pass plays at a high rate without exposing Burrow to too many hits. 

Stat to know: Mims has yielded only five total pressures (one sack, three hits, one hurry) across 334 pass-blocking snaps at right tackle in 2026, posting a pass-blocking efficiency rate of 98.5%.

McKenna: A center? In the top 50?! In this economy!?!? Frazier is, simply, the best player on the Steelers offense. Jaylen Warren is a nice player — perfectly fine. But he’s popping off big runs in large part because of the way Frazier is helping them own the line of scrimmage. It is basically their entire offensive identity. With Aaron Rodgers (and DK Metcalf) looking old, I don’t know how the Steelers would move the ball without Frazier.

Stat to know: Frazier has played 343 pass-blocking snaps at center this season without surrendering a single sack, anchoring Pittsburgh’s interior line with only seven total pressures allowed all year.

Ruiz: Dawkins is the best offensive lineman on perhaps the NFL’s best offensive line. The hulking tackle just wears down defensive linemen in the run game, and he’s a big reason why the Bills' run game has been so successful. There’s a reason head coach Joe Brady loves to call runs to the left side. Dawkins doesn’t have the lightest feet, which can get him into trouble against certain pass rushers, but he’s far from a liability in pass protection. 

Stat to know: Dawkins has allowed just two sacks on 265 pass-blocking snaps this season, and Buffalo's offense has surrendered zero sacks off his edge in five of his seven starts in 2026.

McKenna: The Browns don’t have many elite playmakers, which begs the question of how in the world they’re 5-4. (Credit to Todd Monken!) But Carson Schwesinger is the top dog in Cleveland. They win based on this young defensive core, from Denzel Ward to Schwesinger to Jared Verse. Those are their three playmakers at the three different levels. And DC Mike Rutenberg has each of them playing like some of the best players at their positions.

Stat to know: Schwesinger has posted double-digit total tackles in five separate games this season, leading Cleveland with 89 tackles (40 solo, 49 assisted) while adding 3.0 sacks in nine games.

Ruiz: By Stingley’s standards, 2026 has been a "down year" for the Texans cornerback. He’s still been very good, allowing only 1.1 yards per coverage snap, per Next Gen Stats. Stingley remains sticky in coverage, but a few unfortunate lapses at the catch point have dragged down his numbers. Still, Stingley is as complete a cornerback as you’ll find. He can play man, he can play zone, and few defensive backs can match his ball skills. 

Stat to know: Stingley has broken up at least one pass in six of Houston’s eight games this season. Since 2025, his 22 passes defensed and five interceptions rank among the top three boundary cornerbacks in the AFC.

McKenna: Turner’s ascent has been rapid in 2026. He already has nearly as many sacks this year (7) as he did in 17 games last year (8). And that’s because he’s earned himself a role as an every-down player. Last year, he played just 65% of snaps. This year, he’s up to 80%. That’s why all his statistics are surging, including pressures, where he is tied for fourth in the NFL (41). He’s turning into the perfect queen on Brian Flores’ chessboard.

Stat to know: In his third NFL season, Turner has produced 7.0 sacks and 20 quarterback hits in his first eight games, joining Danielle Hunter as the only Vikings edge rushers in the last decade to reach 20 QB hits prior to Week 10.

Ruiz: Crosby isn’t putting up gaudy sack numbers, but he remains one of the NFL’s most complete edge defenders. He’s a disruptive force who can cave in a pocket or blow up a run play in the backfield. The sack numbers may not be there, but Crosby is due for some positive regression in that category. His 44 pressures rank third behind Rousseau and Hutchinson, per Pro Football Focus. Another underrated aspect of Crosby’s game: he rarely comes off the field. He leads all edge defenders with 505 snaps played. Hutchinson is second at 468. 

Stat to know: Crosby has registered 33 tackles for loss in 24 regular-season games since the start of 2025, leading all NFL defensive edge rushers in backfield stops over the last two seasons.

McKenna: It’s a joy to watch a player ascend in the manner that Watson has. Going back to 2024, he had elite speed and a set of routes that worked well. But he was far from a complete player. And then the Packers spent most of 2025 running the football and containing their passing offense. Watson missed five games, which has always been a part of the issue with him. And it felt like he was on the verge of stringing it all together, if he could stay healthy. Well, viola. Watson has the fourth-most receiving yards and he has seven touchdowns, already tied for his career-high. He can do a multitude of things for the Packers offense, but his ability to create deep separation has made him a meteoric talent in 2026.

Stat to know: Watson has seven touchdown catches through nine games this season and has averaged 17.9 yards per reception on 49 catches, making him the only receiver in the NFL in 2026 with 45-plus catches, 850-plus yards, and seven-plus touchdowns.

Ruiz: You don’t need to be an offensive line expert to watch Nelson’s tape and realize you’re watching a special player. The dude is a bulldozer in human form, displacing defensive linemen with ease and clearing out holes for his running backs. It will be easier to appreciate Nelson’s talent now that he’s playing for a true contender in Seattle. The Seahawks made that move to improve their run game, but Nelson also shores up the team’s pass protection. He’s allowed just seven pressures this season. 

Stat to know: Across 321 pass-blocking snaps split between Indianapolis and Seattle this season, Nelson has not allowed a single sack, extending his streak to 18 consecutive regular-season starts without giving up a quarterback takedown.

McKenna: I don’t get the sense that many folks recognize the monster that Rousseau has developed into. He’s tied for second-most sacks in the NFL at eight. He’s tied for sixth in the NFL in pressures (40). We saw the Bills' defense finally dominate an opponent — albeit Carson Wentz. And I can’t help but wonder if Rousseau and his DC, Jim Leonhard, might be onto something in the second half of the season. Can they keep ascending?

Stat to know: Rousseau has recorded at least one quarterback hit in all eight games this season and has already amassed 25 QB hits and 8.0 sacks, putting him on pace to break Buffalo’s single-season quarterback hits record.

Ruiz: After a slow start to his career, Young is now living up to the pre-draft hype that got him drafted second-overall in 2020. His 8.0 sacks are just behind the league lead, and his 19.7% pass-rush win rate ranks second, per Pro Football Focus. Young is an intimidating presence on the edge of the defense, whether he’s rushing the passer or defending the run. His 34-inch arms let him ward off blockers until it's time to disengage and land an explosive hit on the poor soul with the ball. 

Stat to know: Young has tallied eight sacks through New Orleans’s first eight games this season, recording at least a half-sack in six different contests and matching his career high for sacks in a single season.

McKenna: It’s a double-edged sword with Dak, who has monster years of production (like this one), because Jerry Jones is seemingly only willing to invest in offense. So Dak lights up the scoreboard while his defense lets opponents do the same. And then — tale as old as time — the coach botches the end-of-game situations often enough for the Cowboys to live just below .500. I think Dak has the potential to be a Top 10 player, if paired with a talented head coach. But Brian Schottenheimer isn’t that guy. So here is Dak … a good player. Not a great one.

Stat to know: Prescott has thrown for 250-plus yards in seven of Dallas’s nine games this season. With 16 touchdown passes in 2026, he is one of only four active quarterbacks with eight career seasons of at least 15 passing touchdowns before Week 10.

Ruiz: Whatever questions the Texans had about their quarterback have been answered this season. Stroud has left no doubt: he is a quarterback worth paying. He’s shored up his accuracy, and his play under pressure has improved dramatically. Through the first half, he’s been the NFL’s best quarterback against the blitz. Those were the big concerns that were preventing Houston from going all-in on the 25-year-old. The longer the team waits to pay him, the higher the price will be. Stroud ranks fifth in passer rating, and he’s averaging 8.0 yards per attempt. If he maintains those numbers, he could be the league’s highest-paid quarterback in a few months. 

Stat to know: Stroud has thrown multiple touchdown passes with zero interceptions in five of his eight starts this season, leading the NFL in games with two-plus pass touchdowns and no turnovers.

McKenna: Wright is allowing an absurd 3.77 seconds in time to pressure, with just three sacks allowed. His pressure totals (36) are actually on the high side, but that time to pressure is what excuses Wright (and points more to his QB for holding onto the football). But it’s not just the passing game where Wright excels. He’s a huge part of the Bears’ power run game, where D’Andre Swift is playing out of his mind. Bears coach Ben Johnson loves Wright. It’s why the tackle got a massive extension this offseason. 

Stat to know: Wright has surrendered just one sack and 12 total pressures across 376 pass-blocking snaps at right tackle this season, anchoring a Chicago pass-protection unit with a pressure rate allowed under 3.2%.

Ruiz: Bonitto is behind the statistical pace he’s set the last few years, but he hasn’t been any easier to block. Few offensive tackles can keep up with the fifth-year pro when he fires off the ball. He’s so quick off the line, he doesn’t have to do much hand fighting to get by a blocker. His bend lets him turn the corner to get to the quarterback. The numbers may be down, but Binitto has played his best lately. He could be in for a huge second half. Don’t be surprised if he outplays this ranking down the stretch. 

Stat to know: Bonitto has racked up 18.5 sacks and 39 quarterback hits across 26 regular-season games dating back to Week 1 of 2025, giving him the most multi-sack games (5) on the Denver defense over that span.

McKenna: During the Seahawks’ Super Bowl run, Witherspoon established himself as one of the best cover corners. During the Seahawks’ Super Bowl win, he shocked everyone — especially Drake Maye — by debuting his elite blitzing abilities. Then the Seahawks paid him to keep doing it in Seattle. Which is exactly what has happened. The Seahawks' defense hasn’t been quite as elite. But Witherspoon’s quality of play hasn’t wavered.

Stat to know: Witherspoon has recorded at least five tackles in eight of Seattle's nine games this season. With 56 total tackles and five tackles for loss in 2026, he is one of only two NFL cornerbacks currently leading their team's secondary in both categories.

Ruiz: Lawrence has been everything the Bengals could have hoped for when they traded a first-round pick for him in the offseason. He leads the NFL in run stuffs and has been a productive pass rusher with 29 pressures. Only three interior defensive linemen have generated more. His five sacks tie him for third among that group. Lawrence has been a force multiplier for an overachieving Bengals defensive line, and he’s helped protect the linebackers, the team’s biggest weakness. 

Stat to know: In his first eight games with Cincinnati, Lawrence has compiled 5.0 sacks and eight tackles for loss — the fastest any defensive tackle has reached 5.0 sacks in a debut season with the Bengals since modern sack tracking began in 1982.

McKenna: Despite all the drama surrounding the Myles Garrett trade and his knee injury, McDuffie has quietly done what he always does: play like one of the NFL’s best. He’s not a flashy ballhawk. And he’s a willing run supporter. So there’s a blue-collar way that he plays the cornerback position, which doesn’t always lend itself to praise — or highlights. But McDuffie is one of the few things that have gone right for the Rams in 2026. The acquisition has been massively impactful.

Stat to know: Since joining the Rams, McDuffie has already recorded two interceptions and eight passes defensed through six games in 2026, matching his entire regular-season takeaways total from the previous two seasons combined.

Ruiz: McBride might be the best pure tight end in the NFL. He doesn’t run routes quite like Bowers, but he’s a better in-line blocker. I’m sure some old-school offensive coaches would take him over our TE1. McBride also has the Gronk-like ability to run through a defender’s face. He’s also one of the best red-zone weapons in the NFL.  If he played for a better team — and with a better quarterback — his numbers would look even better. McBride has already hauled in 73 catches at the midway point, but they’ve produced just 598 yards. 

Stat to know: McBride has caught at least seven passes in seven of Arizona’s first nine games this season. After hauling in 126 catches in 2025, his 199 receptions over a 26-game regular-season span are the most by a tight end in NFL history over that stretch.

McKenna: Every quarterback has a weakness. (Everybody has weaknesses.) Goff’s weakness is as clear as day. He struggles against pressure — and more than most QBs. And while there was a phase of the season when he seemed to be getting better, he has actually regressed back to the mean. In his career, his EPA per dropback against pressure is -.33. This year, it’s -.31. That said, the Lions know Goff’s weakness, just like everyone else. And Detroit is doing a better job than usual in preventing pressure, which is why Goff is up here with the league’s best. The Lions are back to highlighting his strengths.

Stat to know: Through his first eight games of the 2026 season, Goff has thrown 15 touchdown passes against only two interceptions, joining Peyton Manning and Aaron Rodgers as the only quarterbacks since 2000 to post multiple career eight-game spans with 15-plus passing touchdowns and two or fewer picks.

Ruiz: Is there a better arm in the league right now? Williams has the finesse of a Patrick Mahomes, the raw power of Josh Allen, and the ability to throw on the move of Lamar Jackson. There are still some noticeable gaps in his game, but Williams is on track to become one of the league’s best quarterbacks. If we re-ranked the top-50 at the end of the season, Williams could crack the top-10. He just needs to shore up his accuracy and avoid the catastrophic performances we saw against Minnesota and Tampa Bay. 

Stat to know: Across his first two seasons, Williams reached 35 career touchdown passes in his 23rd regular-season start, making him the fastest quarterback in Bears franchise history to hit the 35-touchdown milestone.

McKenna: Lamb’s reemergence has been impressive, particularly as we see George Pickens fade back into clear-cut WR2 status. I thought Pickens would eat into Lamb’s workload, if I’m being honest. I thought 1) Pickens was that good, and 2) Pickens would be that motivated with his uncertain contract status. But even with added pressure and motivation from Pickens, it has been Lamb who has reasserted himself as one of the league’s elite receivers. I love the way Lamb plays, with real dominance from every receiver position in the offense. He and Dak Prescott are back to their same old stuff.

Stat to know: Lamb has 70 catches for 904 yards and seven touchdowns, setting the Cowboys' receptions record through both Week 9 and the team’s first nine games. His receiving yardage ranks second in franchise history through Week 9 and third through Dallas’ first nine games.

Ruiz: Higgins may be in Chase’s shadow, but he’s still standing out. Cincinnati’s WR1b. does everything you’d expect out of a premier receiver. He gets open deep, dominates the catch point, and separates against man coverage. He’s also got the strongest hands you’ll find in the league. Higgins is putting up numbers (67 catches, 758 yards, six touchdowns), but he’d be even more productive if he didn’t have to share targets with another superstar pass catcher. 

Stat to know: Higgins has three games with 140 receiving yards or more, which is tied for the most in the NFL this season. He also has a catch of 20 yards or more in six of his eight games. 

McKenna: It will be interesting to see how and if Josh Downs can change the Chiefs' offense. For years, the Chiefs offense has constricted tighter and tighter to the line of scrimmage, with the defense controlling KC’s offense, in large part because of a lack of impact pass-catchers. Travis Kelce’s game is deteriorating. Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy haven’t become the threats that the Chiefs thought they’d be. I’m not totally bought in on the idea that Downs will suddenly realize his potential — particularly when plopped into this offense at midseason. But he can only help. And if he brings something explosive, then we could see Mahomes rise up this list. Because he’s playing well — but mostly stepping aside to let Walker carry the offense.

Stat to know: Earlier this season, Patrick Mahomes earned his 100th career win in his 131st start, tying Tom Brady as the fastest quarterback to reach 100 wins in NFL history.

Ruiz: By the numbers, Ward has been the best cornerback in the NFL this season, allowing only 129 yards on 335 coverage snaps, per Pro Football Focus. That leads all cornerbacks with at least 250 coverage snaps. Ward has been targeted only 36 times this season, and there’s a reason why quarterbacks avoid him. He’s sticky in coverage and will fight receivers for the ball, as evidenced by his three interceptions and three pass breakups. Ward has given up two touchdowns, which pushed him down this list a few spots.  

Stat to know: Ward has allowed a 47.4% completion rate and just 3.8 yards per target on 38 targets in primary coverage, with no touchdowns allowed, three interceptions and nine passes defensed.

McKenna: When a quarterback lines up before the snap, they must account for where Hamilton is on the field. It’s sort of like what Ed Reed was for the Ravens. Different players. But a similar impact. And so a QB must know where Hamilton is at all times. That’s largely because he can be anywhere and do anything for this defense. And if, at any point, the offense loses track of him, it’ll be because he’s about to make a big play.

Stat to know: Hamilton leads all NFL safeties with nine tackles for loss, accounting for 15% of his 60 total tackles. He also has five passes defensed and one interception.

Ruiz: Where would the Rams' passing game be without Nacua? Unfortunately, with him set to miss time, we’re about to find out. But before he got injured, Nacua was doing it all for the Rams. He can move the chains as a reliable possession receiver. He can win on vertical routes on the perimeter. And there isn’t a tougher receiver to bring down after the catch. L.A.’s dependence on Nacua drags down his efficiency, but he was still putting up impressive volume stats before the injury, averaging over 100 receiving yards per game. 

Stat to know: Nacua’s 70 receptions this season are the most through a player’s first seven games of a season in NFL history, breaking Adam Thielen’s record of 67 set in 2018.

McKenna: I’m going to get killed for saying this, but Purdy is starting to remind me of a mini Josh Allen. Even I know that it sounds ridiculous, part of what makes Allen so special is his sheer size. But as you can see in these rankings, a diminutive Allen (like Purdy) can be pretty darn special. He has been excellent in structure, particularly when he had two healthy receivers in Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel. With the entire WR corps getting injured, Purdy has gotten creative out of structure, using his athleticism and arm talent to generate big plays. He has taken a sizable leap in his development over the last 12 months.

Stat to know: Purdy’s 104.8 career passer rating is the highest in NFL history among players with at least 1,500 pass attempts.

Ruiz: If we put together this list before the Week 9 game against the Packers, Gonzalez would have been even higher. He was torched for 187 yards in the game, but had given up just 196 yards in the previous six games, according to Next Gen Stats. Don’t let one bad game fool you: Gonzalez is a lockdown corner who can travel with top wideouts thanks to his length, athleticism, and agility. There isn’t a better man coverage cornerback in the league. 

Stat to know: Gonzalez has not allowed a touchdown on 45 targets as New England’s top boundary cornerback.

McKenna: There’s still nothing he can’t do. Sure, his production is slightly down. But that’s not because Chase is doing anything wrong, per se. It’s just that Tee Higgins has gotten that much better, which means that he’s an absolute vacuum for targets in the Bengals offense. As has been the story for these two receivers, they have to take turns having huge games. And Higgins is enjoying more than he used to. But if you sleep on Chase — even slightly — he’ll do what he did to the Falcons last week: 10 catches, 155 yards and a touchdown.

Stat to know: Joe Burrow and Chase have connected for 19 touchdowns of 40-plus yards, tying Joe Montana and Jerry Rice for the third-most by a QB-WR duo since 1980. Their 58 touchdown connections, including playoffs, moved them past Daunte Culpepper and Randy Moss for the second-most by a QB-receiver duo before both players turned 30.

Ruiz: Green Bay can’t run the ball, and its pass protection unit is among the worst in the league. That kind of offensive environment would break 99.9% of quarterbacks, but Love is thriving. He’s unshakeable in a tight pocket, and his trademark fadeaway throws help him mitigate the constant waves of pressure he faces. Love isn’t just a great thrower. He’s a sharp processor before and after the snap, which also helps him beat the rush. 

Stat to know: Love leads the NFL in passing yards and has 232 more than the next quarterback this season. His 2,618 passing yards is the third most through Week 9 in Green Bay franchise history (since at least 1948). 

McKenna: No one in the NFL has a faster get-off than Watt at .72 seconds, per Next Gen Stats. That’s how he’s gotten home for 7.5 sacks, the second most in the NFL. He also scored his first pick-six this year — to go with three pass breakups. Watt is the star on a Steelers defense that has been the most reliable force to get Pittsburgh to 6-2. He’s the catalyst — more than Aaron Rodgers or Jaylen Warren. 

Stat: Earlier this season, Watt recorded his 10th career interception, joining Julius Peppers as the only players in NFL history to record at least 100-plus career sacks and 10-plus career interceptions.

Ruiz: Hutchinson is Detroit’s lone source of pressure, which makes it easier for opponents to throw extra blockers at him. That hasn’t stopped the 2022 first-round pick from producing, though. His 51 pressures rank second in the NFL, per Pro Football Focus, and he’s on pace for another double-digit sack season. Hutchinson is an athletic freak with a motor that can’t be turned off. That combination makes him a true playmaker on the defensive line. 

Stat to know: Hutchinson is tied with Greg Rousseau for the NFL lead with 57 quarterback pressures on 341 pass-rush snaps. He also has 18 quarterback hits, sixth in the NFL, and five sacks.

McKenna: This is the type of season we’ve been hoping we’d see from Burrow and the Bengals. They didn’t fall into early holes in wins and losses. Their defense isn’t an absolute atrocity. Their offensive line can protect Burrow. The only shortcoming is the run game, which can’t seem to operate. But Burrow and his receivers have overcome that in spades, with one of the most passing offenses in the NFL. I know there’s a lot of hype around the Green Bay receivers, but I’d take the Bengals every time. And I’m sure Burrow would, too.

Stat to know: Burrow has accounted for at least four touchdowns in four straight games, tying Dan Marino (1984), Drew Brees (2018) and Tom Brady (2020) for the second-longest streak since 1970. Only Peyton Manning’s five-game streak in 2004 was longer in NFL history.

Ruiz: Saying a guy plays smaller than his size is not typically a compliment, but it is for Lawrence. No 6-foot-6 quarterback should be as agile as the Jaguars quarterback is. That quickness helps him navigate the pocket and remain a threat as a passer outside of it. As Lawrence gains experience, the inexplicable decisions are decreasing. He’s also shored up his accuracy. The 27-year-old is averaging 8.6 yards per attempt, which leads all quarterbacks with at least six starts. 

Stat to know: Lawrence ranks second in the NFL with a 111.7 passer rating, behind Joe Burrow (114.8), and leads the league with an 8.0% touchdown rate (18 touchdowns on 224 attempts).

McKenna: For all the jokes about the substation, it’s crazy to think that the 49ers have Warner, 10, and Williams, 38, on this list. It’s not just their longevity. It’s that they’re somehow still getting better. Brock Purdy didn’t get sacked until Week 5. 

Stat to know: Williams has allowed just nine pressures (one sack, two hits and six hurries) on 267 pass-blocking snaps so far this season. His 3.37% pressure rate allowed ranks third among left tackles and eighth among all NFL offensive tackles. 

Ruiz: While you can debate the top player at every other position, there’s no question who the top linebacker is. It’s Warner, and he’s held that title for the last few years. If anything, the gap is widening, as the 29-year-old just keeps getting better. He’s the best coverage linebacker in the sport. It’s like the guy has an extra set of eyes on the back of his head when he’s playing zone coverage. And now his run defense is starting to catch up. 

Stat to know: Warner is the only player in NFL history to record 75-plus tackles and 5-plus forced fumbles through Week 9 of a season.

McKenna: Robinson is still among the NFL’s elite, but I’ll admit that I’m surprised to have him at RB3 at this point in the season. And it’s not a matter of the shine coming off one of the best players in the league. He just hasn’t quite done what Gibbs or Walker have done. Because the Falcons are so often engaged in shootouts and/or are playing from behind, he’s not getting the same number of carries. He’s also seeing a humble share of the targets. He's been amazing! But he’s also trailing Gibbs and Walker in basically every statistical category.

Stat to know: Robinson leads the NFL with 880 rushing yards and 665 yards after contact through Week 9. His yards after contact alone exceed the total rushing yards of all but six other NFL running backs.

Ruiz: Bowers may be listed as a tight end, but the Raiders use him as a do-it-all receiving threat. Linebackers and safeties stand no chance of covering him, and cornerbacks don’t fare much better when Bowers splits out wide. He has had some issues staying healthy early in his career, but even with two games missed, Bowers leads all tight ends in receiving yards and is tied for the league lead in touchdowns. 

Stat to know: Bowers surpassed 2,500 receiving yards in his 36th NFL game, becoming the fastest tight end to reach that mark in NFL history, ahead of Kellen Winslow (37 games).

McKenna: He has gone over 100 yards in five of his eight games as a Chief. He has also scored two or more touchdowns in five of his eight games. And it’s not like he’s racking up production based solely on his offensive line. He leads the NFL in rush yards over expected (254), per Next Gen Stats. And he’s just behind Gibbs in missed tackles forced (60). More than all that, he has been one of the most enjoyable players to watch, with the ability to pop at any moment — and against any defensive unit or alignment.

Stat to know: Walker became the second player since 1970 to score multiple touchdowns in four of his first five games of a season, joining Calvin Johnson (2011). Walker also has five games with multiple touchdowns through the first eight games of 2026, tied with Terrell Davis (1998), Emmitt Smith (1995), Eric Dickerson (1983) and Marcus Allen (1982) for the most since the 1970 merger, trailing only Jim Brown’s six in 1958 all-time.

Ruiz: Sewell has made the difficult transition from the right side to the left without a hitch. He’s a monster in the run game and can be used in a variety of ways. He can move defensive linemen on downhill runs or pull outside and block on the move. And while run blocking is his superpower, Sewell’s pass protection is nearly as impressive. He’s allowed just eight pressures and one sack all season. 

Stat to know: Sewell has allowed just nine pressures (one sack, three hits and five hurries) on 309 pass-blocking snaps. His 2.91% pressure rate allowed ranks second among left tackles and fourth among all NFL offensive tackles.

McKenna: Just after the trade, I wrote about how, in Chicago, Simmons would finally get the love he deserves as one of the best — if not the best — defensive tackles in the NFL. And that the seemingly high price would make sense when you saw Simmons on a legit defense and a winning team. Tennessee is the worst place for an elite player, because no one seems to notice them. This is the year of Simmons. He and the Bears are going to make a deep playoff run.

Stat to know: The Bears are 2-0 since adding Simmons, allowing an NFL-best 13.0% third-down conversion rate and 5.03 yards per play, down from 26.1% and 6.25 before the trade.

Ruiz: Jared Goff will get most of the credit for Detroit’s offensive success, but there’s no doubt who serves as the engine of the unit. Everything is built around Gibbs’ ability to generate explosive plays. He leads the NFL in runs of 10 or more yards and has forced more missed tackles than anyone in the league, per Next Gen Stats. Gibbs is difficult to tackle and impossible to catch once he’s out in the open field.  

Stat to know:Gibbs’ 60 career touchdowns are tied with LaDainian Tomlinson for the second-most by any player in his first four NFL seasons, trailing only Terrell Davis (61). Gibbs needs two more to set the record.

McKenna: He’s first in the NFL in sacks (9.5) and second in pressures (44). And in turn, he’s doing everything he can to drag a mediocre Texans defense back into relevance. The defense might be the biggest reason they’re struggling — and in (high) danger of missing the playoffs. But Anderson and C.J. Stroud are the biggest reasons why they can still make a postseason push, despite the statistical improbability.

Stat to know: Anderson leads the NFL with 9.5 sacks, ranks second in tackles for loss (12), and ranks fourth in total pressures (47). His 9.5 sacks are the second-most through Week 9 in Texans franchise history, trailing only J.J. Watt's 10.5 in 2012.

Ruiz: The Seahawks superstar is on track to win the receiving triple crown, leading the league in receptions (71), yards (1,036), and touchdowns (9). And there’s no reason to expect any slippage in the second half. Defenses have no answers for a receiver who gets open at all three levels, wins contested catches, and creates after the catch. There’s no such thing as a perfect player, but JSN gets close. 

Stat to know: Smith-Njigba became the third wide receiver in the Super Bowl era to record at least 800 scrimmage yards and eight touchdowns through his first seven games of a season, joining Cooper Kupp (2021) and Jerry Rice (1986). He has topped 100 receiving yards in seven of nine games this season.

McKenna: There are times when it looks like he’s playing 1 vs. 11 out there — and winning. But this year, he’s also getting his whole team behind him for 11 vs. 11. And that has been when the Bills are unstoppable — when their QB1 leverages the whole offensive unit. Just because he can play hero ball doesn’t mean he should play hero ball. I think he’s getting that, and it’s making him — and the Bills — better.

Stat to know: Allen is the first player in NFL history with at least nine passing touchdowns and nine rushing touchdowns through his team’s first eight games of a season. He has 12 passing touchdowns and nine rushing touchdowns.

title: College Basketball Catchup: Michigan Rebounds, Vandy Got Better, UCLA Is Hot
content:
Michigan bounced back after a loss to UConn. A second-year forward looks like she's taking the leap for Mississippi State. UCLA is hot, hot, hot to start the season.

Here's what you need to know from yesterday's slate of college basketball.

Michigan is in a tough position. At least, relative to a year ago, when the Wolverines were one of the top teams for almost the entire season, and then ended up being national champions. Now, though, Michigan has a new coach — Mike Boynton — and some new players, too, and lost to UConn already.

On Wednesday, Michigan faced off against Marquette at home, and came away with an 84-70 victory. Tennessee transfer J.P. Estrella played a significant role, with the senior forward scoring 18 with eight rebounds and two assists in his 31 minutes, but right up there with Estrella was freshman Quinn Costello. In 25 minutes off the bench, the forward scored 15 points, all on threes: he was 5-for-6 from beyond the arc, and didn’t shoot once from inside it.

Mike Boynton had nothing but positive things to say about Costello postgame. "I’ve coached some really good shooters, I’ve never coached a 6’10" guy who can shoot like he can."

Boyton explained that Costello is a "high achiever" who works hard on the non-shooting aspects of his game to help the team win, but on Wednesday it was absolutely his shot that helped Michigan the most. 

Mississippi State’s Favour Nwaedozi is no stranger to rebounding. As a junior last year, the 6-foot-3 forward — who had arrived for her first NCAA season after spending two years playing for Mukogawa Women’s University in Japan — pulled down exactly 10 boards per game, and did so while averaging 12.2 points per, as well. That’s averaging a double-double right there.

On Wednesday against Troy, Nwaedozi was right back at it, only better. She had eight rebounds just about halfway into the first quarter, and would finish the night with 19 boards and 22 points.

Nwaedozi had an assist and two steals just for good measure, and shot 10-for-14 while scoring another two from the line for the top showing of the day. She currently leads all players in the SEC with 14.7 rebounds per game as well as total boards, with 44, and what’s most wild about that is she’s playing about 22 minutes per game. Her per 40 minute numbers are cartoonish: Nwaedozi is averaging 25.9 rebounds per game there. Just three games, yes, but in her second season in the SEC, a better performance than an already great one wouldn’t be a surprise.

Ethan Roberts joined Notre Dame history last night, sinking 10 threes in 13 attempts — he’s one of just three Fighting Irish, along with Kyle McAlarney and Matt Farrell, to make 10 threes in a single game.

Roberts didn’t just score from deep, even if that was mostly where his points came from. He added another six from inside the arc to lead all scorers, men and women, on Wednesday. Notre Dame didn’t need quite that level of performance out of Roberts — the Irish defeated South Carolina State, 99-59 — but they got it all the same.

Roberts is the first D-I men’s hooper this year to hit double-digit threes, but not the first D-I  player to accomplish the feat in 2026: Chloe Donnell dropped 14 against Ecclesia for Northwestern State on Nov. 2. Roberts is, however, the first of the year to manage it against a Division I opponent instead of a team from a lower division.

Unlike with Notre Dame and Roberts, the women’s scoring leader on Wednesday absolutely needed to go that hard in order for her team to win. Nadia Moore, a junior guard from Duquesne who has only this year become a regular starter, dropped a career-best 33 against Marist in a game the Dukes would win by a mere five points.

Moore started hot, and finished scorching: she scored 15 of Duquesne’s 22 points in the fourth quarter, in a game the Dukes would win 72-67. She helped out with more than just pure scoring, too, as Moore dished out four assists, grabbed a steal and secured five rebounds, and shot accurately at 69% overall and 4-for-7 on treys.

She had never scored even 20 points in a game before, with her previous career-best sitting at 18. Coming into Wednesday, Moore had just three games on her résumé in which she scored more points than she did in the fourth quarter of this one alone. Marist certainly wasn’t ready for that shift.

Mia Woolfolk had two pretty good seasons for Georgia before transferring to Vanderbilt for the 2026-2027 season. With the Commodores, she’s going to have more help than she did on the Bulldogs, and Woolfolk is also going to make Vandy better than it was, too. Against Western Kentucky last night, Woolfolk was unstoppable in the paint. She took 14 shots and missed just two, sank three of four from the charity stripe, and grabbed three boards and a steal while she was busy in the paint, too.

Sophomore guard Aubrey Galvan — see above clip — is already enjoying having Woolfolk hanging around in the paint as another scoring option to pass to, and her constant threat there is going to create opportunities for All-American Mikayla Blakes to take better shots this season, too: a terrifying proposition, considering Blakes led Division I in scoring last season with 27 points per game.

No. 9 UCLA is off to a terrific start this year. The Bruins have averaged 101.3 points per game across their first three contests, dropping 84, 114 and 106 points so far. That 84 was no joke, either, because it came against then-No. 5 Arizona in the Bruins’ first dub of the season.

UCLA’s women’s team is the defending national champion; the men’s team hasn’t won since the 1994-1995 season, however, when the Bruins won their still-men’s-record 11th title. Mick Cronin’s squad has quite a bit of season left to get through, but that win against Arizona and the subsequent beatdown against opponents the Bruins should be winning is at least making this team seem like one that has something to show the rest of the league this year.

title: How to Watch Commanders vs. Giants: TV Channel, Live Stream, Time
content:
The Washington Commanders visit the New York Giants in Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at 8:15 p.m. ET from MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

The Giants lead the NFC East by two games after a 19-11 win at Philadelphia on Nov. 8, their second straight victory, and they hold the NFC's No. 3 seed at 5-2-1.

Washington has fallen three games behind New York after a 20-13 loss to the Rams on Nov. 8 left it at 2-5-1. A loss on a short week would drop the Commanders four games back of their division rival with eight games left, while a win would pull them within two.

Below are the details on how to watch.

Washington has thrown one interception as a team, and none came on Jayden Daniels' 180 attempts. He has 1,250 passing yards and seven touchdowns in six games and has run for 252 yards and two more scores.

He threw for 300 yards and two touchdowns at San Francisco on Oct. 19, but he has also been sacked 16 times. The Giants allow 177.8 passing yards a game, the third-fewest in the NFL, so Daniels may need his legs and some patience against a defense that gives up little through the air.

Washington's backfield is a committee, but Rachaad White is the one who catches the ball, with 18 receptions and two receiving touchdowns. Both are more than any other back on the roster.

He has run for 228 yards and a touchdown on 54 carries, with a season high of 55 yards in the 27-10 win over the Eagles on Nov. 1. The Giants allow 123.6 rushing yards a game, more than 20 other teams, so White should find early room and give Daniels some play-action help.

Protection is the question for J.J. McCarthy, who has thrown for 622 yards but has been sacked nine times in four games. He has one touchdown pass and averages 9.1 yards an attempt.

A hip pointer limited him early in the week, but he was a full participant in practice Tuesday and is expected to play. Washington has 37 quarterback hurries, the third-most in the NFL, so McCarthy will need his line to hold up long enough to keep pushing the ball downfield.

Washington has already seen Malik Nabers draw 20 targets in a game. He had 11 catches for 121 yards and a touchdown in the 27-27 tie on Oct. 11, the most targets he has had in a game this season.

He leads the Giants with 648 receiving yards, and his season high is 165 on 12 catches against the Saints on Oct. 18. Washington allows 240 passing yards a game, the third-most in the NFL, so Nabers should keep getting chances to produce.

title: Roll The Tape: Can Kirk Cousins Save The Vikings' Super Bowl Hopes?
content:
The Minnesota Vikings have a new quarterback. The Green Bay Packers might have the most dangerous duo on offense. The Los Angeles Rams finally have their dominant duo on defense. 

Each week, I dive into the All-22 coaches' film before offering a few insights to watch. Here are three developments that could be long-term storylines involving some of the best teams and players in the NFL.

Christmas came early for the Vikings, who received a huge gift in the form of Kirk Cousins via a desperate trade with the Las Vegas Raiders. The deal reunites Minnesota's old QB1 with Kevin O’Connell, as the frustrated head coach and offensive playcaller tries to revive a dormant offense that has scored only 11 offensive touchdowns this season. 

Although some would call a third-round pick a hefty price for a 38-year-old quarterback nearing the end of his NFL run, the Vikings’ putrid offense has desperately needed a point guard to spread the ball around to a collection of electric playmakers who have been stymied by miserable quarterback play since the start of the 2025 season. 

While Kyler Murray was expected to jumpstart the unit, the two-time Pro Bowler has been injured and ineffective since Week 1. And with Carson Wentz virtually unplayable as a fill-in on Monday night, the Vikings were forced to bring back their old franchise quarterback to see if he can save their title hopes with rock-solid pocket play. 

Despite coming off his worst performance of the season in Week 9 against the 49ers, Cousins is an upgrade over his predecessors because of his scheme knowledge and willingness to force-feed the ball to Justin Jefferson on the perimeter. The veteran enjoyed a stellar run with KOC in 2022, throwing for 4,547 yards and 29 touchdowns while leading Minnesota to a 13-4 record. Jefferson was the biggest beneficiary of Cousins' presence, earning Offensive Player of the Year honors after tallying 128 receptions, 1,809 receiving yards and eight touchdowns. Cousins was producing at an even more prolific rate in 2023 through eight games (2,331 yards, 18 TDs, 5 INTs) before tearing his Achilles, which marked the end of his first stint with the Vikings.

While it is unlikely Cousins can hit those numbers at his advanced age, he arrives in Minneapolis having thrown for multiple touchdowns in seven of his nine starts with the Raiders this season. As a touch-and-timing passer with great anticipation, Cousins will enable KOC to work the middle of the field with traditional drop-back and play-action concepts. Additionally, his familiarity with the offense should allow the Vikings to use the back pages of the playbook, leading to more "scheme it up" touchdowns to wideouts Jefferson and Jordan Addison and tight end T.J. Hockenson on exotic play designs. 

With Cousins also understanding the nuances of the system and how to get the offense into the perfect call against bastardized looks, the Vikings’ overall efficiency should improve with a better pre-snap process at the line. Whether that means calling a run into a "light box" or checking into the perfect "hot" route to counter a blitz, Cousins’ experience and expertise should bode well for an offense that has struggled to move the ball, much less put points on the board. 

Granted, KOC and Cousins will need time to get on the same page after spending so much time apart, but the chemistry and connection between the playcaller and playmaker should lead to better play from a unit that simply requires competent quarterback play. While achieving postseason success with Cousins is a daunting challenge (he has won just one of his four career postseason starts, and those were all during his prime), the 6-2 Vikings desperately needed the veteran back to give them a chance to make a run this year. 

Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love has emerged as an MVP candidate in 2026, but the ascension of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden as the league’s most explosive receiving duo is currently generating just as much buzz within league circles. 

While the Packers’ co-WR1s have been impressive throughout the season, their Week 9 dismantling of Pro Bowl cornerback Christian Gonzalez and the New England Patriots has evaluators singing their praises. In helping the Packers earn a 45-27 win, Watson and Golden became the first teammates to finish with 150-plus receiving yards and a touchdown since 2023. Moreover, they put on a 60-minute exhibition of superior route-running and playmaking that should serve as teaching tape for aspiring receivers looking to elevate their games. 

Watson is the classic vertical receiver on the outside, with his size, speed and length creating mismatches on the perimeter. The fifth-year pro is a blur on downfield routes, using his long strides and sneaky acceleration to blow past defenders. Measuring at 6-foot-4, 208 pounds, with a verified 4.36 40 time at the 2022 NFL Scouting Combine, Watson leads the league with 17 big-play catches (20-plus yards) while averaging 17.9 yards per catch and 97.7 receiving yards per game. 

Watson has developed into one of the deep-ball specialists in the business, sporting a 50% catch rate on passes covering 20-plus air yards (nine receptions on 18 targets for 354 yards) and a 39.3 yards-per-catch average on those throws in 2026, per Next Gen Stats. 

The 5-foot-11 Golden is nearly as productive as an explosive playmaker with 14 "big-play" snags, tied for the fourth-most in the NFL. As a high-volume receiver, the 2025 first-rounder specializes in getting open using crafty releases and top-of-the-route moves to create significant separation at the break point. He is sneaky effective as a downfield target, averaging 41.3 yards per catch on seven receptions that covered at least 20 air yards. Additionally, he is averaging 87.0 receiving yards per game.

Although his catch rate is less than ideal (57.6%), Golden makes up for his inconsistencies with spectacular "catch-and-run" plays, logging 245 YAC (yards after catch) yards, which ranks 17th in the NFL. With the 6-3 Packers relying heavily on the passing game to move the ball because of their struggles on the ground, the emerging duo is showing up and showing out as arguably the best 1-2 receiving punch in football. 

It took until Week 9 for the football world to see the collaboration that defensive enthusiasts had been waiting for as superstar defensive linemen Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald lined up beside one another against the Washington Commanders. The future gold jacket wearers have combined for five Defensive Player of the Year awards, 13 first-team All-Pro selections, 239.5 total sacks and 328 tackles for loss between them.  

Even with Donald in the twilight of his career, the sight of No. 99 alongside No. 95 on the Rams’ defensive front changes everything for opponents. Garrett’s speed, explosiveness and athleticism from the edges overwhelm offensive tackles, while Donald can still wreak havoc on interior blockers with his strength, power and relentless effort. The perennial All-Pros routinely have their way with blockers, using a mix of finesse and power moves to get to the quarterback on pivotal downs.  

Against the Commanders, we finally got a chance to catch a glimpse of how Garrett and Donald would work together at the point of attack. The results were spectacular: The Rams held the Commanders to 5.0 yards per play while registering four sacks on the 23 snaps they were on the field together. Compared to the 8.0 yards per play and the touchdown allowed during the 19 plays they were both off the field, the Rams’ defensive resurgence, sparked by the veterans, will force the rest of the league to take notice. 

Garrett, who generated six pressures and three sacks on 27 pass rushes (22.2% pressure rate), looked like the reigning Defensive Player of the Year in his first action since Week 1. He looked fully back from knee surgery, whipping the Commanders’ offensive line with basketball moves he’s patented at the line of scrimmage. Whether it was the classic "Euro-step" on his strip-sack of Jayden Daniels (his first sack of the game) or the crossover move that led to his third sack, Garrett’s freakish athleticism creates problems for lumbering defenders at the line. 

Schematically, Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula used a hardwood concept to create favorable matchups for Garrett to tap into his hoops repertoire on the grass. On Garrett's third sack of the game, the Rams aligned in a "Double Eagle" front with the five-time All-Pro positioned over the center at five yards depth. Donald and defensive end Braden Fiske (No. 55) lined up outside the offensive guards, with outside linebackers Byron Young (No. 0) and Josaiah Stewart (No. 10) aligned on the outside shoulders of the offensive tackle. The pre-snap alignment isolated Garrett at center, with Donald and Fiske creating a bigger runway by taking outside releases to the offensive tackles after the snap. 

With Young and Stewart bluffing and bailing into coverage, the Rams won with a three-man rush that gave Garrett plenty of room to work over Commanders center Matt Glubin with a hesitation "dip-and-rip" move or a crossover that showcased his athleticism and basketball skills in the clutch. 

Although the Commanders’ game was a showcase for Garrett, Donald’s presence at the line of scrimmage is noteworthy as well. The veteran has generated multiple pressures in each of the past five games, and his pressure rate has increased despite not registering a sack yet. 

With the Rams’ offensive firepower potentially muted by Davante Adams and Puka Nacua on the sidelines, the defensive front’s resurgence might be enough to salvage the club's playoff hopes.

title: Colin Cowherd On Indiana: ‘The Offense Is A BB Gun Without Fernando Mendoza’
content:
Colin Cowherd thinks Curt Cignetti got too much of the credit for Indiana’s national championship, and he says the Hoosiers’ recent offense is evidence of it.

On Wednesday’s episode of "The Herd," Cowherd said the quarterback who led that title run, Fernando Mendoza, who is now the starter for the Las Vegas Raiders, deserved at least half of it. 

Cowherd's comments come as the defending champions prepare to host No. 18 USC on Saturday. Indiana fell five spots to No. 9 in the latest College Football Playoff rankings during its bye week.

"Under Curt Cignetti, the offense is a BB gun without Fernando Mendoza," Cowherd said. "He’s a really, really good coach. But he’s not [Nick] Saban."

Cowherd began by saying he works for a company with a stake in the Big Ten, and that he loves the Cignetti story.

"I think the Curt Cignetti story is awesome. I think it’s been a little overplayed," Cowherd said. "I thought he got about 90% of the credit for their national championship, and I think Mendoza deserved at least half of it."

He pointed to Cignetti’s 35-3 record since taking over at Indiana. But he added Indiana is different from the Alabama teams Nick Saban built.

"His record is otherworldly. It’s 35-3 as he took over a bad program," Cowherd said. "He’s a really, really good coach, but he’s not Saban. Saban, both sides of the ball. Players became irrelevant at Alabama. Offense, defense, you couldn’t separate them. They were great at both. That’s not what Indiana is. Indiana, he sets a very high floor foundationally and culturally. Mendoza was the ceiling."

Cowherd pointed to Indiana’s record against ranked opponents with and without Mendoza.

"If you look at Indiana against ranked opponents under Curt Cignetti, when Mendoza played, they averaged 38 a game and win by three touchdowns," Cowherd said. "Without Mendoza, including this year, they’re 0-3 and they score 15 points. Mendoza against ranked teams is 6-0 and dropping 38."

He also questioned Cignetti’s offensive philosophy and the 16-0 team.

"Cignetti is super conservative. Nick Saban was not offensively. He’s not the recruiter of Saban," Cowherd said. "I think he’s a very, very good coach, but he got an incredible amount of the love on that 16-0 team that could have easily lost five games if Mendoza wasn’t the quarterback."

Cowherd said that isn’t a knock on Cignetti, and he doesn’t think Mendoza will be Peyton Manning, but he did say he wouldn’t be surprised if USC wins Saturday.

"I would not be shocked if they lost to USC. I really wouldn’t. They’re both off a bye. I wouldn’t be shocked," Cowherd said. "I think USC’s got much more firepower offensively."

When asked about Indiana dropping in the rankings, Cowherd named three teams he thinks can win the national title this season.

"I don’t spend a lot of time on where these are ranked," Cowherd said. "I think Georgia, Notre Dame, Miami are the only three teams that can win a national championship."
